title: Unit – 5 : Session – 9 : SLO – 1  |  Applications of Graphs
sections: I. Fill in the Blanks
A GRAPH is a collection of vertices connected by edges.
GPS navigation systems use DIJKSTRA'S algorithm to find the shortest path.
A DIRECTED graph has edges with direction associated with them.
KRUSKAL'S / PRIM'S algorithm is used to find a Minimum Spanning Tree in a graph.
Social media platforms can be modeled using UNDIRECTED (friendship) or DIRECTED (follow) graphs.
II. True or False
Dijkstra's algorithm works with graphs having negative edge weights — FALSE.
In social networks, people can be represented as nodes — TRUE.
A tree is a special case of a graph that contains cycles — FALSE (a tree is acyclic).
Graphs are not useful in real-world applications — FALSE.
Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms are used to find the shortest path in a graph — FALSE (they find the MST).
III. Match the Following
1. Web page linking — b) Directed Graph
2. Telephone network optimization — d) Kruskal's Algorithm
3. Flight route planning — c) Dijkstra's Algorithm
4. Cable TV wiring — a) Minimum Spanning Tree
5. GPS Navigation — e) Weighted Graph (with Dijkstra's shortest path)
IV. Short Answer Questions
1. Graph: a set of vertices connected by edges, G = (V, E). Applications: social networks, road networks/GPS.
2. Google Maps/GPS: intersections and locations are vertices, roads are weighted edges (distance/time);
Dijkstra's (or A*) computes the shortest/fastest route between source and destination.
3. Directed vs undirected: directed edges are one-way (u -> v), undirected edges are mutual (u - v).
4. MST: a subset of edges connecting all vertices with minimum total weight and no cycles; used in network
design — laying cables, pipelines, and electrical grids at minimum cost.
5. Computer networks: routers/computers are vertices, links are weighted edges (latency/bandwidth);
routing protocols use shortest-path algorithms; network design uses MSTs.
